asVictim.foundWith: his hands still taped, and a fight program in his pocket with his name spelled wrong.

doing.text: laying a fringed cloth on a round table for a sitting
polishing a crystal ball with the hem of her skirt
staring at a spot just over a stranger’s left shoulder
touching a lace handkerchief to her temples, as if somebody were calling
looking at the wedding rings in the case as if listening to them
eating a steak alone at a corner table with her eyes shut

looks.text: A large, soft woman in purple at a round table with a fringed cloth, in a room lit by one red bulb, with her eyes closed and her rings on.
A voice that drops an octave when she wants it to, and a lace handkerchief she touches to her temples when the dead are being difficult.
Dark eyes made up darker, and a little silver bell on a chain at her wrist that rings when she gestures, which is often.

ask: You want my evening. I felt you would. Sit. Take my hands. No? As you like.
The spirits keep strange hours, and so do I. But I’ll tell you mine.
deflect: The other side is silent on that, and so am I.
I see a great deal. I don’t say all of it. It’s bad for business and worse for the dead.
nobodyElse: That’s all. Nobody living, I should say.
That’s all. The room was empty, as far as you’d be able to tell.

hours.7: Seven is when the veil is thinnest. Also it’s after supper, so the clients are calmer.
hours.8: Eight, I sit very still and wait for somebody to speak. Usually it’s the people downstairs.
hours.9: Nine, I have a little sherry. For the nerves. The dead can be very demanding.
hours.10: Ten, I feel things. Tonight I felt a draft, mostly.
hours.11: Eleven, I put out the red bulb and put on the ordinary one, and I’m an ordinary woman for an hour.

refuse: No. Some messages are for one person only, and you’re not the person.
The spirits say no, and for once I agree with them.
ownUp: Very well. Even a medium has to come back to earth sometime. Here it is.

ties.line: Mr. Glick sells people their funerals and I sell them what comes after, and he says I’m eating into his business.
Mrs. Rafferty comes to my table in a veil so the priest won’t know her, and her husband comes through every time, complaining. A very reliable spirit.
Mrs. Sobel calls me a fraud on every stoop on Orchard Street. I could tell her who her husband talks to now, but I’m above it.
Lazar Belkin courted me in nineteen-ten with a voice like an organ and a ring he borrowed back. I saw it coming. That’s my gift.
Mr. Mabry owes me two dollars for a future. He’s welcome to it; it’s a good one.
Dr. Hirsch says the spirits are nerves. She has never once come to my table, which is how I know she’s afraid of what they’d say.
Mrs. Pomerantz lends me her wooden heads for sittings. A wooden head on the shelf is very good for the atmosphere.

secrets.text: She buys dead men’s watches and letters out of the back room at Wexler’s, so that the dead have something to say at her table.
She eats a steak alone at Steinmetz’s every Friday, though she tells her clients the spirits forbid her meat.

asVictim.why: Half the widows on the East Side have told her things at her table they never told their husbands, alive or otherwise.
asVictim.foundWith: her rings still on and a lace handkerchief in one hand, and a talking board on the table with its pointer on GOODBYE.

doing.text: letting out the seams of the rabbi’s costume again
pricing a fur collar with her fingertips, eyes shut
threading a needle on the first try without looking
measuring a stranger by eye and telling him his size
pressing a costume on an ironing board in her kitchen

looks.text: A stout woman in a black smock with a tape measure round her neck like a stole, sitting among the costume racks with a needle going.
A thimble on one finger she never takes off, even to eat, worn so thin you can see the nail through it.
Little gold scissors on a ribbon at her waist, and a pocketful of buttons that rattle when she laughs.

ask: My evening, darling? I sewed. Ask me what I sewed; it’s more interesting.
Sit, sit, mind the pins. I’ll give it to you stitch by stitch.
deflect: I see clothes, not people. People come and go. A good coat, I remember.
Ask me about a hem, I’ll talk all night. About that, I know nothing.
nobodyElse: Nobody else, darling. Me and forty costumes and a dragon.
That’s all. Not a soul came down. The stairs are steep, and actors are lazy.

hours.7: Seven, the actors come down for their costumes, and I count them out like a librarian.
hours.8: Eight, the curtain goes up, and I sit down for the first time since breakfast.
hours.9: Nine, the second act, and somebody always splits something. Tonight the czar.
hours.10: Ten, I mend what the first two acts did.
hours.11: Eleven, the costumes come back, and I count them in, and one is always missing a button.

refuse: No. I’m sewing my lips shut, and I do a very neat stitch.
That I don’t alter.
ownUp: All right, darling. I’ll unpick the whole seam for you.

ties.line: Mr. Belkin pays me on Fridays when there’s money and on Mondays when there isn’t, and every week he wants his costume let out and my bill taken in.
Tillie is the only one in the company who says thank you for a hem, so she gets the good thread.
Mr. Pinsky thinks a theater is the seats. I know it’s the costumes. We argue about it on the stairs between the acts.
Mr. Wexler hangs a coat in a back room for a year. I put it on a king the same night. Which of us loves a coat?
Bertha Krantz and I share a landing and a newspaper. She reads the rents and I read the deaths, and we swap at the funnies.

secrets.text: She lends the Lyric’s dinner jackets out by the night to men who need one for an evening and no questions, and has them back on the rack by the matinee.

asVictim.why: She has bought half the wardrobe at the Lyric off men who stole it, and she keeps the receipts sewn into the hems.
asVictim.foundWith: a tape measure round her neck and a mink collar in her lap with a price ticket still on it.

doing.text: opening oysters faster than anybody could eat them
holding a stranger’s ring up to the light behind the oyster bar
singing under his breath about a girl from Galway
picking a sliver of shell out of his thumb with a pin
eating his supper at the back of the stove with his boots off

looks.text: A long, red-haired Irishman in a rubber apron behind the oyster bar, with a short blade in one hand, an oyster in the other and a cigarette in the corner of his mouth.
Hands nicked all over from the shells, and a row of rings on his little finger, none of which fit.
A green bow tie and a voice like a priest at a christening.

ask: Ah, sure. Pull up a stool and I’ll open you a dozen while I talk; they’re no use to anybody shut.
My evening, is it? It went by opening oysters, and that’s the truth of it.
deflect: I open oysters. What’s inside people, I leave shut.
Ask me no questions and I’ll open you no lies.
nobodyElse: Nobody else at the bar. Just me and a barrel of Blue Points.
That’s the lot. If there’d been another, I’d have sold him a dozen.

hours.7: Seven, the oysters come in on ice off the boat, and I have a word with each one.
hours.8: Eight, the oyster bar fills with men who think an oyster will make them younger.
hours.9: Nine, the theater crowd, wanting half a dozen and the check before they’ve sat down.
hours.10: Ten, I’ve opened four hundred, and my hands are telling me about every one.
hours.11: Eleven, the men short of the price of a steak come up to the bar and show me their rings. I’m a kind man, God help me.

refuse: No. That one’s staying in its shell.
I’ll not open that one. It might be bad.
ownUp: All right. Out it comes, the whole thing, on the half shell.

ties.line: Mrs. Rafferty took me in when I came over from Galway with one suit and a cough, and she’s been curing the both of them since.
Mrs. Greco feeds me in her kitchen at midnight and calls me a heathen for the length of the plate.
Demos thinks a chop house is a cathedral and he’s the bishop. I think it’s a place a man eats an oyster.
Young Lieb offers a man two dollars for his ring and a lecture. I offer him three and a dozen Blue Points.
Agnes and I walked out a few times, till she found I work nights and I found she does too, and now we see each other on the stairs.

secrets.text: He keeps the rings he buys in a barrel of ice under the oyster bar at Steinmetz’s, and the police have leaned on the barrel twice.

asVictim.why: He has bought a ring off every man on Grand Street who ever ran short of the price of a steak, and some of them want it back.
asVictim.foundWith: an oyster blade in his apron pocket and a handful of wedding rings, none of them his.

doing.text: sitting by the oil stove with a cigar box on his knees
stacking chips into a tray in fives
wiping his hands on a rag that made them dirtier
listening to an engine nobody else could hear
taking a clock to pieces on newspaper on the kitchen table
drinking tea with lemon at the bar like a man in mourning

looks.text: A bald old man in greasy overalls and a good gray vest, by the oil stove with a cigar box on his knees and his hands black to the wrist.
Grease in every line of his face, so that he looks like a photograph of himself left out in the rain.
A cigar box under his arm that he never puts down, and never opens in company.

ask: What. Ask.
My night. I sat. The el went by. Write that down a hundred times.
deflect: I fix cars. People, I don’t open the hood.
Ask upstairs. Downstairs we don’t know nothing.
nobodyElse: That’s all. Cars don’t count.
That’s all. Nobody came near the stove but the cold.

hours.7: Seven, I shut the garage doors and put the chain on.
hours.8: Eight, I go up and light the stove in the card room. A cold player is a slow player.
hours.9: Nine, I sit by the stove. The losers come to me after. I’m very patient.
hours.10: Ten, the el stops for a minute and you can hear the chips. Then it starts again.
hours.11: Eleven, the first one is broke. He comes over to the stove with his watch in his hand. I always have tea.

refuse: No. Go and lose your money like a gentleman.
No. That one I’m not opening up.
ownUp: All right. I’ll tell you, and then I’ll have my tea.

ties.line: Russo owes the garage two months for the room upstairs, and I collect it for the boss. I don’t ask. I sit by his stove and wait for his customers.
Teitel and I came over on the same boat in ’88. He went into neckties and I went into horses, and then the horses went into automobiles.
Amato owes six weeks for keeping his cab in the garage, and he parks it like he’s angry at it.
Wexler gives a man a ticket and a month. I give him tea and cash. Which one does he come back to?

secrets.text: He keeps the losers’ watches in a coffee can under the floor of the garage, and has never sold one, in case.

asVictim.why: He has bought the watch off every man who ever lost his last hand at the card room, and some of those men want it back.
asVictim.foundWith: a cigar box on his knees full of other men’s watches, every one of them stopped.
